sections.h2: What is different about selling inside Metro Nashville's single government?
sections.html:
Since 1963 the city and Davidson County have run as one Metro government, which puts valuation, billing and deed recording for a sale under one roof. Only Belle Meade, Ridgetop and Goodlettsville levy a separate city tax of their own. Terrain matters too: the Cumberland River cuts through the Nashville Basin while the Highland Rim hills ring the west, so listings often mention slopes and retaining walls.

Census Bureau figures for mid-2025 show 721,074 residents in the Nashville-Davidson balance, a 4.6% rise over the 2020 base. Owners occupy just 52.4% of homes, so landlords, heirs and people changing jobs make up a big slice of sellers. Use the table to see which Metro desk answers which question.

Metro officeWhat it doesWhere to reach it
Register of DeedsRecords the deed, collects the state transfer levy300 Deaderick St; open Monday to Friday, 8 to 4:30
TrusteePrints tax statements, takes paymentHoward Office Building, Suite 220
Assessor of PropertySets each parcel's appraised value615-862-6080
Codes AdministrationPermits short term rentalsApplications and rules on nashville.gov

Table details come from the Register of Deeds and the Trustee's FAQ.

sections.h2: What does Census data reveal about housing in Nashville?
sections.html:
For 2020 to 2024, QuickFacts shows a median owner-occupied value of $413,600 and a median rent of $1,586. There are 313,513 households here, averaging 2.13 people, and 80.7% of residents stayed put over the previous year.

  • Median household income: $77,371 in 2024 dollars
  • College graduates, 25 and older: 48.0%
  • Average commute: 24.7 minutes each way
  • Share of people in poverty: 14.1%

Averages hide a lot. A downtown condo and a ranch house in Antioch sit far apart, so study comparable sales near your address before choosing a price. The figures come from Census QuickFacts.

sections.h2: Why did Nashville tax bills jump after the 2025 reappraisal?
sections.html:
Values were mailed on April 18, 2025 and the median parcel rose 45%, with council district medians running from 38% to 54%. The state first trimmed the old rates to revenue-neutral levels, according to the Assessor, and then Metro raised them again: owners in the Urban Services District pay $2.814 for each $100 assessed, and those in the General Services District pay $2.782. Those are jumps of 26% and 39% over the certified rates. Only the value is open to appeal.

State law taxes a house on 25% of its appraised value. Run the Census median of $413,600 through that and the taxable amount is about $103,400, and the Trustee's method yields roughly $2,909 in the Urban Services District or $2,876 elsewhere in the county. The 2025 windows, May 9 for informal reviews and June 27 for formal appeals, have closed. For future cycles, ask the Assessor's appraisal staff at 615-862-6059.

sections.h2: What will the Trustee's bill look like when I close?
sections.html:
The Trustee prints the annual statement for the parcel's owner of record, and it covers the whole calendar year. Your title company should divide it on the settlement sheet. Unpaid amounts follow the parcel, so confirm that the year is settled before you hand over keys.

  • Statements go out in early October, and the first Monday of October is the due date.
  • Interest-free payment runs to the end of February.
  • From March 1 the Trustee adds 1.5% per month.
  • A card payment adds 2.55% (minimum $2.00); an e-check adds $1.00.

No Tennessee rule obliges the Trustee to mail a notice, so a lost bill does not pause interest. Parcels that stay delinquent go to a tax sale auction, with a one-year redemption right for the owner.

sections.h2: Does Nashville offer property tax relief that a seller should mention?
sections.html:
For owners 65 and up there is a freeze, and low-income elderly or disabled owners and disabled veterans can claim relief. The Comptroller's 2026 table caps freeze income at $54,900 here. A veteran rated 100% disabled has no income test, and the relief applies to the first $175,000 of market value.

Mention any of these to the buyer's side early, so the settlement figures reflect the real bill. The Trustee's office at 615-862-6330 can say which proofs of age, residence and income it wants.

sections.h2: What happens at the Register of Deeds on Deaderick Street?
sections.html:
The office at 300 Deaderick Street files deeds and also accepts remote filings. The state adds 37 cents for every $100 of price on the transfer. It takes original documents with notarized signatures, and its staff cannot draft a deed or search for liens. Hire a title company or attorney for that.

Anyone can search the indexes in the office, and online access is sold by subscription. Ask the closer to record on the day you sign so the new deed is indexed quickly, and request a certified copy later if you need one for your files.

sections.h2: Does a short term rental permit stay with a Nashville house?
sections.html:
It does not. Metro Codes ties the permit to a named holder and one address, and any change of owner cancels it, including a move from a person into a trust or LLC. Anyone wanting nightly guests must file from scratch.

  • A permit lapses 365 days after issue unless renewed.
  • The guest count tops out at twice the sleeping rooms plus four, never more than 12.
  • Renters must be 21 or older.
  • Three code violations can cost the holder the permit.

Put the permit status in your offer paperwork. The Metro Codes operating rules spell out every condition.

sections.h2: What is the story behind Nashville's older neighborhoods?
sections.html:
Settlers built Fort Nashborough in 1779 beside the Cumberland. The town was incorporated in 1806, became the state's permanent capital in 1843, and a Metro charter joined it to the county in 1963. Nashville's public schools date to Hume School in 1855, and the unified Metro district now lists 160 schools, including 12 zoned high schools that run career-focused Academies of Nashville and a set of magnet schools with themes such as arts, languages and sciences. Families moving in often ask whether a house is zoned for a magnet option, and MNPS can answer that for a specific address.

Housing from many eras sits side by side. Sellers of older houses can pull the year built and living area from the Assessor's record and check them against the listing. Roof age, foundation movement and old wiring are the items buyers most often ask about, so price those in or fix them before showings.

sections.h2: What are the quickest ways to sell a Nashville house?
sections.html:
Listing the house draws the biggest crowd of buyers, along with showings, appraisals and repair demands. Selling to a cash buyer who takes the house in its current state gives up some of that reach for speed, because closing waits on title work rather than a lender.

Whichever you choose, get the price in writing, state in the contract who pays the recording tax, and have a title company prepare and file the deed. Deal with liens, back taxes and any rental permit questions before closing day.

faqs.q: Will I owe Davidson County tax if I sell in November?
faqs.a: Yes, for the months you owned it. The bill covers all of the calendar year, and the settlement statement should split it between you and the buyer.

faqs.q: Can a Nashville owner contest the tax rate?
faqs.a: No. The Assessor says only values can be appealed, and the Mayor and Metro Council set the rate. The 2025 figures were $2.814 and $2.782 for the two service districts.

faqs.q: How much does the state charge to record a Nashville deed?
faqs.a: The transfer tax is $0.37 per $100 of price, and the state recording fee has a $10 minimum. The Register of Deeds has an online calculator for exact totals.

faqs.q: Can a buyer take over my short term rental permit?
faqs.a: No. Metro Codes bars assignment to another person, entity or address, and a change of ownership cancels the permit. The new owner must apply again.

faqs.q: Where can I pay Metro property tax in person?
faqs.a: At the Trustee's office, Suite 220 of the Howard Office Building, 700 President Ronald Reagan Way. Hours are weekdays 8:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. Mail goes to PO Box 196358, Nashville, TN 37219-6358.
